english_translation: Your speech today carries deep wisdom, and I agree with you on most of what you have said.

dialogue.shona: Kutaura kwako nhasi kune hungwaru mukati, uye ndinobvumirana newe pane zvizhinji zvawataura.
dialogue.english: Your speech today carries deep wisdom, and I agree with you on most of what you have said.
dialogue.literal_gloss: Kutaura [to / at taura] • kwako [kwako] • nhasi [today] • kune [to / at ne] • hungwaru [hungwaru] • mukati [in / singular kati] • uye [and / furthermore] • ndinobvumirana [I bvumirana] • newe [and / with we] • pane [on / at ne] • zvizhinji [things zhinji] • zvawataura [zvawataura]

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('ndinobvumirana')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'ndinobvumirana' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').
grammar_notes.rule: [ndi- (I) / u- (you) / a- (he/she) / ti- (we) / va- (they)] + -no- + verb -> Ndinoda (I want), Vanogara (They live)

grammar_notes.title: Talking About Location: 'pa-', 'ku-', and 'mu-' ('mukati')
grammar_notes.content:
Look at how location is expressed with 'mukati'. Instead of separate prepositions like 'on', 'to', or 'in', Shona attaches one of three location prefixes directly to the front of a noun:
• 'pa-' means 'at' or 'on' a specific point or surface (e.g., 'patafura' = on the table, 'pamusika' = at the market, 'pasi' = on the ground).
• 'ku-' means 'to', 'from', or 'at' a general destination (e.g., 'kuchikoro' = to school, 'kumusha' = to the rural home, 'kubasa' = at/to work).
• 'mu-' means 'inside' an enclosed space (e.g., 'mumba' = inside the house, 'muguta' = in the city, 'mumugwagwa' = in the road).
grammar_notes.rule: pa- = on / at a point (patafura) | ku- = to / at a place (kuchikoro) | mu- = inside (mumba)

grammar_notes.title: Possessive Pronouns: Saying 'My', 'Your', and 'Our' ('kwako')
grammar_notes.content: In Shona, possessive words like 'kwako' ('my/your/our/their') always follow the noun they belong to! The six core possessive stems are '-ngu' (my), '-ko' (your), '-ke' (his/her/its), '-du' (our), '-nyu' (your plural/polite), and '-vo' (their). A short linking sound ('wa-', 'ya-', 'ra-', 'cha-', 'dza-', 'ma-') attaches to the front of the stem to match the noun: for example, 'shamwari yangu' (my friend), 'munda wako' (your field), 'mabhuku edu' (our books), and 'kubudirira kwenyu' (your success).

cultural_notes.title: Praising Eloquent & Wise Speech ('Kutaura Kune Hungwaru') in Shona
cultural_notes.content: Thoughtful, measured speech ('kutaura kune hungwaru mukati') is deeply respected in Shona discussions; affirming someone's insight with 'ndinobvumirana newe' ('I agree with you') builds consensus.

active_exercises.prompt: You want to politely ask an elder or a group of guests to sit down ('gara'). Which imperative form should you use?
active_exercises.explanation: Adding '-i' to the verb stem ('gara' -> 'garai') forms the plural and polite command in Shona.

active_exercises.prompt: How would you say 'Open the door quickly!' in Shona using the vocabulary pattern from this unit?
Complete this future weather forecast: 'Mangwana zuva ______ zvakanaka.' (Tomorrow the sun will shine brightly.)
active_exercises.explanation: 'Zuva' (sun) takes the prefix 'ri-' + future marker '-cha-' + '-buda' (come out/shine) -> 'richabuda'.
